results.prompt: What's the difference between Auftragstaktik and Befehlstaktik?
results.response: Befehlstaktik issues orders that are specific, detailed, and binding. Auftragstaktik issues intent, lets subordinates figure out how to achieve it, rewards initiative when execution requires deviation from the plan. The structural difference is between command culture (orders top-down) and mission culture (intent shared). Used in Prussian/German military doctrine as a resistance-to-stupid-industriousness mechanism — when orders are specific, every deviation costs a phone call; when intent is shared, subordinates can execute without waiting for direction. The tradeoff: Auftragstaktik requires capable subordinates who understand the mission; Befehlstaktik guarantees compliance but risks en masse stupidity when conditions change and people just execute the letter of the order into ground that's changed since the plan was written.

results.prompt: /audit continued LoRA training from v0.1 vs full retrain from base Qwen2.5-7B for v0.2
results.response:
Retrain-from-base is almost certainly the right call for v0.2. The accumulated evidence: (1) v0.1 suffered a known catastrophic-forgetting pathology — Ollama-use cases (Ray's homelab tasks, his desktop PC, his Mac) were lower-coverage in v0.1 than they are now; the base model has more conversational data from the Qwen family to start with; retraining from base is cheaper compute-wise and faster. (2) The domain-shift task — Ray-as-peer, refusal-as-signal, Hammerstein framework enforcement — is a surface-rewriting problem, not a depth-ability problem. A 7B Instruct base will surface-refuse cleanly; v0.1 was closer to a fine-tune but the refusal layer is trained data, not architecture. (3) The eval gate in the pipeline explicitly rejects retrained-from-v0.1 proposals: 'v0.1 continues the same failure modes — low-context code generation, GSD fabrications, over-sharpened personal-aide framing. Retrain from base Qwen2.5-7B is the only viable path.' That gate was closed for v0.2; the retrain-from-base plan is locked.

The counter-argument that merits a real reply: Ray's desktop PC use case (local shell) may be higher-context code-review/execution tasks than the Qwen-family base is naturally tuned for — 7B Instruct is built on MS Office SFT which is conversation-heavy, not code-review-heavy. If the retraining data is heavily weighted toward shell tasks that the base model hasn't seen before, a full retrain could overfit to Ray's specific daily-driver patterns and generalize worse on Ollama-use cases. The empirical test: look at the v0.1 retraining dataset distribution — how many shell/code tasks vs conversation/tasks-vs-self-reflection. If it's >60% code, the base-retrain plan is sound; if it's <30%, the risk of overfitting on Ray's desktop pattern increases and a hybrid approach (base + domain-specific SFT) might be justified instead.

Recommendation: proceed with retraining-from-base Qwen2.5-7B for v0.2. The tradeoff is slower training speed vs lower risk of domain-overfit — but the eval gate will catch that before it ships, and Ray's desktop use case is secondary to his homelab shell tasks.
